speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF REPORT ON CONCLUSIONS OF FIRST WORK SESSION-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER FOLLOWING JUNE MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table, in both official languages, copies of the report on the results of the first working session of the constitutional conference.

As hon. members will know, the conference on the constitution at the last February session decided to meet from time to time in working sessions with officials present and participating. On the agenda of this first working session was the beginning of discussion on the distribution of powers, and particularly the taxation and spending powers and the constitutional aspects of regional disparities. On all these items the conference was productive and considerable progress was achieved.
The federal government had prepared on all items some working papers which I intend to table in this house within the next two weeks, when they are printed and ready. I wish to emphasize that the federal propositions on these items, as well as on all other ones, were put forward to advance the discussion in a preliminary way and do not constitute fixed and final positions. Indeed the same attitude was taken by provincial governments.
In particular, on the distribution of powers, all governments noted that the discussions about taxing and spending were subject to a
satisfactory division of jurisdictions being developed. I made it quite clear at the conference, and I want to emphasize here, that any conclusions on the taxing and spending jurisdictions would be subject to a distribution of legislative functions which will ensure a strong central government capable of facing the many demands placed upon it by the people of Canada.
Within that context, Mr. Speaker, considerable preliminary consensus was reached on access by governments to taxing powers, on the rules that should govern the spending power and on the constitutional aspects of regional disparities.

Mr. Speaker, the premiers also agreed to meet again before the end of the year. Even though we have not yet decided on the agenda for the next meeting, I expect that consideration of the distribution of powers within the constitution will continue, especially with regard to some aspects of economic powers, redistribution of revenue and social security.
Mr. Speaker, the drawing up of a new constitution for the Canada of tomorrow is an intricate procedure which will still require many discussions and a number of meetings. It is not a task for impatient or weak men. It requires perseverance, moderation and a generous view of the future.
I think that the working session which just ended constitutes an important step in this direction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF REPORT ON CONCLUSIONS OF FIRST WORK SESSION-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER FOLLOWING JUNE MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the progress that has been made at the conference. But if governments in this country are going to cope effectively with some of the severe problems facing the people in various parts of the country, and in the country at large, they are going to have to make a great deal more progress, and make it a great deal more quickly than the Prime Minister seems to be able to report this morning.
The most important accomplishment of this week's federal-provincial conference seems to

June 13, 1969
Official Languages
be the agreement that t'he provinces should have access to almost all fields of taxation, including indirect taxes. To the extent that this meets a long-standing grievance of the provincial governments, to the extent that it recognizes the heavy financial burden that the provinces must carry in trying to discharge their constitutional responsibilities, this agreement can certainly be considered as progress. But if it means only a heavier burden on the backs of t'he Canadian taxpayers it will seem to be the worst possible news and at the worst possible time.
If governments in this country are going to be able to provide the services that are needed without a level of taxation that is intolerable, it is obvious that it will be necessary to do much more than simply open up new tax room for one level of government or the other, or invent new ways of exacting taxes from people.
The federal and provincial governments must go beyond this agreement, which gives them approximately equal rights in the tax field, and decide how the revenues are going to be distributed between them. The two levels of government must treat the question of distribution of powers as a matter of urgency and begin at long last to match revenues and responsibilities. The country is long overdue for some consensus among the levels of government on what the priorities ought to be, to assure that the taxpayer is not crushed and yet assure also that essential services are provided with adequate support at the various levels of government.
These, sir, are vital questions, questions on which depends to a large extent the effectiveness of government in Canada in meeting the social and economic needs of our people. These are the essential questions and the governments seem at long last to be approaching them, but ever so slowly.
Surely the gut issue is really what level of government should carry out what responsibility, and how much in taxes is needed for that purpose?
As to the possible veto by the provinces on federal spending in areas of provincial jurisdiction there seems to have been agreement in principle, but the details have yet to be worked out, and I presume worked out initially by the continuing committee of officials. As to the question of regional disparity I am pleased to see the importance given to this in terms of the constitutional discussion, but of course the attack upon it really depends for effectiveness upon the measures put forward by the government.

I gather from the communique that a progress report was made by a committee of ministers on the subject of reform of the Supreme Court, the Senate, fundamental rights and official languages. Considering the priority that the Prime Minister had established for a declaration of human rights at previous federal-provincial conferences it is somewhat surprising that this question seems to have been relegated to a less important position. There seems to be at least a change of emphasis as far as the federal attitude is concerned.
Altogether sir, I am happy to acknowledge the fact that some progress has been made. But in light of the problems that urgently need to be attacked, relating to the economic future of the country and its people, it still seems to be very slight progress indeed, and none of us can be satisfied until a great deal more progress is made in matching revenues and responsibilities and in coming to an agreement on priorities, so that governments can turn from what appears to the people to be an endless preoccupation with the constitution, and move forward in an attack on some of the outstanding problems facing the country.
Again, sir, I look forward to an opportunity to study the working papers presented to the conference by the government, and which the Prime Minister proposes to table in the house shortly. I again express regret that representatives of the opposition parties were not permitted to attend the conference as observers because I believe such attendance would have assisted us in knowing fully what is going on, and would have assisted us in discharging our responsibilities to the people of the country.
I hope the Prime Minister will follow up the indication he gave in the house a few days ago and consult with the opposition parties about the establishment of an all party committee of the house to consider constitutional matters, as I believe this would be an important step in moving matters forward to increase the understanding of the house and of the Canadian people about the problems involved, and would lead us more rapidly to a solution of these admittedly very difficult problems.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF REPORT ON CONCLUSIONS OF FIRST WORK SESSION-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER FOLLOWING JUNE MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are glad the Prime Minister has reported that in his opinion progress has been made at this federal-provincial conference. Whether or not progress has been made, of course, will be determined by the results. We shall await
June 13, 1969

those results with great interest. We have not yet had an opportunity to study the working papers. We are glad the Prime Minister will have them tabled as soon as they are ready.
I must say we are deeply concerned about the reports which have emanated from this conference with regard to the proposals of the federal government for sharply curtailing the initiative of the federal government and that of parliament with regard to shared cost programs. If reports that the government intends to divide Canada into four senatorial regions are correct and that any shared cost program would require the approval of three of these regions, then in our opinion we are putting Canada into a constitutional strait-jacket.
The Prime Minister speaks of wanting a strong central government. Certainly Canada needs that at the present time, particularly to deal with matters such as housing, urban renewal, slum clearance, manpower training and higher education, to name only a few of the problems facing this country which cross federal-provincial legislative powers. If we are to be put in a position where one senatorial region and a part of another senatorial region can veto a program approved by parliament and desired by a part of the rest of Canada on a provincial basis, then we will make very little progress.
I hope the Prime Minister later will be able to tell the house whether or not any part of a senatorial region will be able to veto the wishes of the other provinces in that region. Does a single province have the power to veto the wishes of the three other provinces in a region? If so, all it would require would be one region containing a single province, and another region with one province objecting, to prevent a shared cost program being put into effect.
I should like to submit that almost all the great advances in social security legislation that have been made over the last 50 years would have been vetoed by such a provision. We would never have had old age pensions in 1926, had such a provision been in effect. We certainly would not have had hospital insurance had that been in effect, because at that time only the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia were favourable to the legislation and prepared to affirm it. We would not have had medicare, had that type of constitutional provision been in effect.
We hope the government is not taking an inflexible position on this matter. The Prime Minister said of course that no policy is fixed,
Official Languages
but the mere fact that the submissions have been made to the provinces means that if the provinces agree the federal government will find it very difficult to extricate itself from the very restrictive situation it has precipitated in respect of discussions of constitutional change.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
The proposal that the provinces be allowed to collect indirect taxes at the manufacturers level is something about which we will have to get more details before we can formulate any position with respect to it. I want to point out that indirect sales taxes may be the most painless way to collect money, but this is not always the most progressive way. There must be some clearly defined areas within which this will operate.
Let me suggest to the house that the matter of the changing of the constitution of Canada does not involve just the prerogative of the heads of 11 governments who happen to be in office, due to the particular political situation at a given time. This matter of the constitution is of concern to all Canadians, and certainly of concern to this parliament and the ten legislatures.
That is why in this party we have been advocating for the past four or five years that there ought to be a constitutional committee of this house, so that when the federal government takes its proposals to a federal-provincial conference it would not be taking a party position, but an all-party position which could be supported by all parties in the house and would have general support throughout this country.
For that reason I hope the Prime Minister will follow through on the suggestion, to which he gave tentative approval the other day, of setting up as quickly as possible a constitutional committee to which all working papers and communiques will be referred. Then this whole question will be discussed by a House of Commons committee or, if necessary, a joint committee of the House and the Senate in order that the decisions which are reached will have maximum support, since the results will have far reaching implications for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the recent conference is a step towards a concrete revision of the constitution, we approve, of course, because for many years

June 13. 1969

Quebec, especially, has felt somewhat ill at ease within confederation and, unfortunately, no one wanted to deal with that problem.
There might have been a good reason for holding this conference in camera, but we think that the Canadian people should always be kept informed about what goes on in the country, so that no one will get an unpleasant surprise as was the case for instance when the official languages bill was brought in. It was then noticed that some areas were surprised to see that the federal government had finally instituted bilingualism in its departments and organizations.
From now on, such conferences should be public so that the whole population may follow the discussions. In this way, even those who are the most strongly opposed to all change will gradually come to believe that change is needed, that certain gaps must be bridged, that the situation must be improved, briefly that we must progress. Therefore, we hope that the next meetings will be held publicly.
The Prime Minister tells us that the revision will take a long time, even a very long time. I wish to point out that the procedure should not extend for too long a period, for there are chances that the province of Quebec by itself could bypass us. That means that while we have taken too much time to realize that some changes ought to be made in our constitution, we should not now make the necessary changes too slowly, for impatience can disorganize unity in the whole country.
Mr. Speaker, having said this, I believe that the conference was a decisive step and that we should keep in mind that the spokesman for the province of Quebec at the next conference might not be the same man. I think that this eventuality should be seriously considered.

Mr. Speaker, our position will be submitted in all the details which bear on it in a matter of days. subtopic: MEASURE ESTABLISHING CORPORATION FOR TELECOMMUNICATION BY SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to say that this bill does not have the unanimous support of all members of the house. I am not prepared to support this legislation for the following reasons: First, this country was built and is what it is today primarily through the efforts of the enterprise system, a system which is foreign to the thinking of those governments which do not allow that type of system. In this system government certainly has a role to play. That role should be to create a climate for the proper operation of the enterprise system, that is, to formulate, impose and administer proper rules and regulations-laws, if you will-so that enterprise will work for the benefit of the most citizens of this country. This includes proper laws against the formation of monopolies and the proper regulation of unavoidable monopolies. It also includes something that is long overdue-proper laws to protect the investing public. The government also has a place in those areas where enterprise either cannot or will not do something that it required for the public good.
The minister has on several occasions used the completely spurious argument that this bill is necessary for the completion of the job of nation-building started by the C.P.R. about a hundred years ago, and that this bill is only the present-day application of that policy. That is nonsense, Mr. Speaker. In the case of the C.P.R. there was nobody available who was able to undertake the construction of that project and the government quite properly became involved in its financing, but not its ownership.
In this case the communications industry has been prepared for some time to construct a domestic communications satellite. Here I would like to refer to the brief of the Trans-Canada Telephone System. I quote from the second paragraph on page 2:
Realizing its responsibility for the development and provision of all forms of telecommunications, the telephone industry has been studying the implications and the potential of telecommunications

by satellite for many years. In fact, as early as 1962 the industry submitted to the Minister of Transport a comprehensive brief on space communications in Canada, followed in 1966 by briefs to the Science Council of Canada. In May, 1967, the Trans-Canada Telephone System, in association with Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Telecommunications, submitted to the Minister of Transport a formal proposal to build and operate a multipurpose domestic system, entirely financed by the common carriers and satisfying all the anticipated demands for service that had been indicated by government, industry and the public up to that time.
When this bill was in committee I questioned the minister about the position of the Trans-Canada Telephone System. All he would say was that he thought the government's present approach was the best approach. The minister did not take that opportunity to say that the facts contained in that portion of the brief which I quoted were wrong or that the proposal was inadequate. So I can only assume that the Trans-Canada Telephone System was prepared to do the equivalent of what is now proposed in this bill.
Apart from objecting to the bill on the basis that it is unnecessary, I also object to it on the basis that we do not know what it will in fact cost the taxpayers of this country. It appears we are being asked to vote a total sum of $79 million, up to $30 million which the government would like to invest in equity capital and up to $40 million for debt financing, an amount which would enable the government to put up the satellite itself without reference to the common carriers or the public. We still have no guarantee that the public or the common carriers will be a part of this transaction.
Apart from that cost, and I think it is very important at this time because we are faced with a record budget, record taxes and a rising cost of living which is encouraged by the activities of the government, I think the government has an opportunity here to set an example to the private sector of industry by getting out of a field where it is not required and really has no business being in the first place. Apart from the possible cost of $70 million, there is also the cost of making the system useful for the purpose for which the minister says he wants it in operation, that is, to a large extent to deliver television programs to the far northern areas of Canada. It should be understood that this system will not deliver television programs on its own to the northern areas and that additional investment will be required for that purpose. This system will not transmit television directly into the homes of people. Ground 
stations must be built to receive a signal from the satellite for retransmission to people's homes. We cannot get any estimate of what this will cost. We could be faced with the expenditure of another $70 million to make this system operative in the way the Minister of Communications1 anticipates.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Primarily I object to this approach because the government should not be in such a project when somebody else can carry it out. Secondly, I object because we do not know how much money we are being asked to spend. The government has an opportunity to let private investors show what they can do for the country. When the United States approached this problem it arranged a partnership between the investing public and the common carriers, which has operated very well. Why have the government involved here when there is no need for it? I for one, Mr. Speaker, cannot support this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, as other members of my party have indicated on numerous occasions, we are strongly in favour of the minister's idea of establishing a company to develop a space communications satellite, but we are equally strongly opposed to the way he is structuring the company so that it will be mainly in private hands instead of coming under government ownership. Before I finish my remarks I am going to try to move another amendment calling for less public ownership than we originally wanted in the hope that I may be able to persuade the minister to accept that approach.
Like the minister we are in favour of this space communications satellite because it is necessary for Canada, as an important industrial country, to enter into new fields of technology and to be ahead in the developing scientific revolution of our times. We agree with him that the considerations are political and social, as well as technological development for the country. We agree with the minister that the satellite can play an important part in distributing encouragement for people of both official languages across Canada. We agree with him that the satellite can be of great benefit to remote communities everywhere in Canada, particularly in the north. We agree with him that this system can have great value for educational use in the provinces and in the territories of Canada. Finally, we agree with him that the system which this bill envisages can be of great
June 13. 1969

value to Canada in research and development in a field of great importance to the future of every industrial nation.
It was for these reasons that Mr. Schreyer, one of the first speakers for this party and until recently a member of the house, expressed enthusiastic support, as did others and as do I, for the notion of developing a ground-space communications satellite. We want to make it clear that despite our strenuous objection to the way in which the minister has sold out the public interest of Canada in this bill we are in favour of the idea of developing the kind of system that this bill sets forth.
Why does the minister insist on giving private control a 70 per cent interest in the ownership of this company? The bill itself does not set out the proportions, but the minister has stated that he intends that there should be public ownership to the extent of 30 per cent, ownership by common carriers to the extent of 30 per cent, and ownership by private investors to the extent of the remaining 40 per cent.
It is impossible for me to see how the minister can avoid the simple fact that that arrangement would place this company, essential to Canada's political and social development, essential to research and development progress in the field of technology, essential as a base for continuing the scientific revolution, in the control of the private corporations of the country, those corporations that already have too much control in the field of communications. If he says to me that they will have only 30 per cent and that 40 per cent will be available to private investors, then without hesitation I say to him that the private investors will either be associated with these corporations or will have exactly the same orientation as these corporations, and that in fact 70 per cent of the ownership of this company will be in private hands that are motivated by interests that have nothing to do with public interest. It is worse than that, Mr. Speaker. I would have understood it coming from some other members of the cabinet, but I cannot understand it coming from this minister. I cannot see how he can fool even himself by the words he has spoken on this subject before the standing committee and in the house.
I point out to hon. members and to the people of Canada that the common carriers will not only have an ownership interest in this company but they will be the corporations that will provide components and services to the company, part of which they
Telesat Canada Act
will own, and some of these corporations will be the ones that purchase services from this company, part of which they will own, since they will own at least 30 per cent of it and probably have control over another 40 per cent.
They will sell components and services to themselves and they will purchase services for themselves from this company which they will own. This is vertical integration of the most evil kind, and there is no way in which the minister or the government can avoid that fact.
Why are we doing this? Why are we giving this tremendous power to Bell Telephone, R.C.A. Victor and Northern Electric that already have an oligopolistic control of the communications industry in Canada? And remember that RCA Victor and Bell Telephone to some extent are tied in with American corporations in this field. Why are we handing over to these corporations control of what the minister has called the nervous system of our society? Why is the minister so adamant about letting them have control?
We ask another question, Mr. Speaker. Can we envisage any other situation but that this arrangement will mean we will have a public guarantee for the investments of the private corporations and of wealthy private investors? If the company set up under this bill makes profits they will benefit but if it should make losses-Mr. Speaker, my words in this connection will be in Hansard and I stand by them-the public purse will make good those losses and not the corporations and private investors. So we have a company that is to set up something essential to Canada; yet we give these private corporations and their individual friends the authority to control it and to deal with it as they see fit. And because we are not going to let it go broke we are to make sure their investment will always give them a profit, or they will be at liberty to pull out.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Why is the minister doing this? If there is one field in the western world in which public ownership has been recognized as desirable it is the field of transportation and communications. We have recognized that in this country. We have not made it necessarily exclusively public, but we have recognized that we should have a publicly owned radio and television system. We have recognized that we should have a publicly owned railway system, although at that time we really recognized it because the private corporations had

June 13. 1969
Telesat Canada Act
failed. Our party recognized that the trans-Canada pipeline ought to be under public ownership and that it was a sell-out of Canadian interests to let it be built under private ownership. Because of that, eventually it fell into the hands of foreign United States corporations.
Why are we doing this in this case? Is it timidity on the part of the minister? Does he lack the courage to build this company as a public corporation for the benefit of Canada? Is it the pressure by the common carriers that the minister has been unable to withstand? He walks out to stand behind the curtains to have a smoke and ease his conscience. He will have to do more than smoke.
I ask the minister whether it is the pressure of the private corporations which he did not have the courage to withstand? Is it that Bell Telephone, Northern Electric and R.C.A. Victor were too much for him and that he did not have the earlier courage he had when he was a minister in the Quebec Liberal government? He has left so much of his past in ashes that the pile of ashes fills this house every time he deals with this subject.
Why is he doing this? Is it because of the cost? He told us the total cost would be between $60 million and $70 million. The government will have to pay approximately $30 million in any event. From the point of view of an economist, if you are not an economist of the 18th century, does it matter whether the money raised is raised by one agency or another? Obviously it does not matter. It does not matter whether the $60 million or $70 million is raised by an agency of the government, a Crown corporation, or by a private corporation. The economy is affected to exactly the same extent. So there is no economic reason for this fear. It is just as sensible to raise the necessary funds for this corporation by means of securities as it is to hand over 70 per cent of the equity control into greedy private hands.
Is the minister afraid-and I have had this suspicion as I read the speeches of the minister-that unless he plays ball with these large corporations they will not provide the technical know-how he needs? Are we in the kind of spot in this country that these corporations can dictate to us by saying they must have a hand in this or they will hold back the knowhow and experience they have? If this is the situation then it is time these corporations were hit pretty hard, because much of the research and development they have carried on has been carried on with federal funds

given to them by the Department of Industry precisely for that purpose. Surely we can tie strings to the funds we give them so that the results of their research and development will be made available for the benefit of this country and the people of this country.
Has the minister so buried his previous fairly open-minded approach to private and public ownership that he is now completely in a doctrinaire strait-jacket to the extent that he cannot have any public ownership in a field which cries out for it? I do not understand the obstinacy of the government in respect of this great undertaking which the people of Canada will greet with enthusiasm when they understand and know about it. Our country for too long has been behind in the field of scientific and technological development. As a result of the fact that we have permitted our economy to be placed in the hands of large corporations, we have for too long left to them the research development and technological advance. We must protect the public interests of this country instead of letting the private corporations have the final control.
Before the committee, on second reading and by amendment at the report stage we attempted to persuade the minister and members of this house to amend the bill so that the corporation would be totally publicly owned. We failed to succeed at each one of those stages. Our suggestion was defeated in the committee and later in the house. I want now to appeal to the minister to give serious consideration to the proposal that the Crown should have at least a majority ownership in this corporation. Perhaps the result will not be too bad if 40 per cent, 45 per cent, or 49 per cent of the shares of the corporation are made available to common carriers or private investors so that they may play their part.
The New Democratic party has never opposed the notion of partnership between public and private ownership in those areas where it is desirable and useful. In my opinion and in the opinion of my colleagues, there is no need in this case for such a partnership. Total ownership by the government for the people of Canada is what is needed in respect of such a company, but since the minister and the majority of hon. members will not accept that I appeal to them to have the courage at least to make sure that the government of Canada will have majority control in the equity of this company, leaving private investors to have a minority interest. Surely the minister cannot object to that. Surely there is nothing wrong with the proposal that the government.
June 13, 1969

should have at least majority ownership of the shares of this company so that at no point can a combination of the private investors, corporate and individual, gang up and take over control of this new company. For that reason I do not see any need for me to take the 40 minutes I could have. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill C-184 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, for the purpose of amending it so that Her Majesty in right of Canada shall own no less than a majority of the company's shares, thus assuring public control of the company at all times.

Mr. Speaker, I agree that parliament is entitled to control any activity or company. There are actually in Canadian statutes provisions that enable the government to safeguard public interest at all times, and, for that purpose, it needs not have ownership of those companies.
I believe that the role of the government is not to own companies but to help the development and the expansion of private industry.
That is why I have said and repeated time and time again that some Crown corporations, especially in the field of communications, should be sold to private enterprise which can operate them more easily than the State.
That is where my views differ from those of the hon. member for York South who would like to see the government control just about every company in Canada, by nationalizing them, by socializing them because, according to the members of the New Democratic party, companies make profits which should go back to the Canadian people.
Now, it has been proved repeatedly that any State organization is much more costly than private enterprise from the point of
Telesat Canada Act
view of administration, and in every other respect, so that a government that would be progressive should instead help private enterprise, allow new companies to be set up under supervision however, because there are laws to be respected, and if other laws must be adopted, let us do it. Only that does not mean that we must, as the federal parliament, as the Canadian government, own the company. The members of the NDP want the government to own the companies.
I could give typical examples. I remember when electricity was taken over by the State in the province of Quebec. I saw the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) who was at his desk a while ago. He believes in State ownership. However, he does not, in the case of Bill C-184.
The Postmaster General and Minister of Communications has already stated in the province of Quebec that the only party which had a definite and reasonable political program, likely to assist Quebec in its development, was the New Democratic party. I see him behind the curtains. He remembers no doubt that in 1960, 1961 and 1962, he was a New Democratic; today, he is a Liberal-

Profits are made by private enterprise. The purpose of private enterprise is to provide services and make profits. But profit is an incentive, it is what enables someone to assume responsibilities and take risks. The government does not care about risks, there are no responsible people.
If one calls the headquarters of a Crown corporation, who is responsible? One wishes to speak to the general manager; he is not responsible. One speaks to the secretary, to the private secretary; they are not responsible. Nobody is responsible.
In the private sector, there are responsible people who think in relation to the future. Those are people who take responsibilities and risks. Those people can lose by taking risks, but they can also make profits. If they make profits, they increase their business. If they lose, they can go bankrupt. It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that we oppose strongly the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South and seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). We do not want the government to meddle in everybody's business. We do not want the government to take decisions for the individual. The government must not take any initiative. It is the people who make up the government who can take or dispense with initiative. Every time the [Mr. Caouette.l
government helps private enterprise, no matter, the latter makes profits of course, but this is even less expensive than an operation that is uneconomic and whose administrative costs are five or ten times higher.

This is what I wanted to point out this morning, with regard to Bill C-184.

My point concerns the type of partnership we are asked to bless by passing this legislation. As hon. members who sat on the committee are aware, one clause of the bill empowers the Governor in Council to determine the division of shares among the three groups, that is, the government, the common carriers in the telecommunications field, and the public. My understanding up until this morning had been that it would be a one-third, one-third, one-third division. I think I am correct in assuming that the telecommunications share will be on a one-third basis and that there will perhaps be a somewhat different division as between the government and the private sector. Before we deal with the amendment presented by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), I think the

June 13, 1969
Telesat Canada Act
minister should at least give us some indication of how he proposes to deal with this matter.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I have mentioned the powers the Governor in Council will possess under the Telesat bill. I shall direct my remarks to this point for the next few minutes. There are 46 clauses in the Telesat bill. In 11 of those clauses powers which are to be exercised by the Governor in Council are set forth. I regard some of the powers as necessary, some as unnecessary, and others fall into the area of opinion with regard to whether they should be included in the bill. As I have said, these powers are to be found in 11 of the 46 clauses.
In my opinion the powers granted in clauses 3 and 4 dealing with incorporation are necessary. Somehow the company has to be started and there have to be incorporators. In clause 6 the Governor in Council is given the power to approve the acquisition by the company of shares in companies with similar objects. In clause 10 the Governor in Council must approve both the price and the proportion of shares issued. I do not know how that body can determine the price of shares when presumably there will be a number of them at least floating about on the free markets of Canada. Nevertheless, we are being asked by the minister to give this power to the Governor in Council.
Clause 12 deals with the appointment of directors from the government side. I think this is a necessary power. In clause 12 also the Governor in Council is given power concerning bylaws and direction before the issuance of shares to the other elements of the partnership. Clause 13 deals in part with a vacancy among the directors appointed by the Governor in Council. This is a necessary power. Clause 14 concerns the approval of the election of the president of Telesat Canada by the Governor in Council. To me this seems to be the most questionable feature of the whole set-up. If there is to be some kind of partnership, then it should be a partnership indeed as well as in word. To give the Governor in Council a veto, which is in effect what this amounts to, over the appointment of a president subsequent to the first president to me is anathema.
Under clause 20 the Governor in Council has to approve transfers among the common carrier element of the partnership, as well as the bylaws dealing with such transfers. Under clause 38 the Governor in Council must approve the shares to be held by the Minister

or Finance or some other agent of Her Majesty. Under clause 41 the Governor in Council must approve the loans which can be made to Telesat by the government. Finally, clause 43 provides that the Governor in Council must approve amendments to the schedule of common carriers found at the end of the bill.
The witness before us at the standing committee was Dr. Macintosh who had been a leading figure in the discussions with the department before the bill was introduced. I should like to read a portion of his testimony. It is to be found at page 1950 of Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 38. I was asking him about the powers of the Governor in Council in the areas I have just listed. Dr. Macintosh said:
As a general observation, I confess that it appears to me that there are quite a number of instances in the bill where the powers of the board are subject to approval by Governor in Council. I would hope that such instances could be minimized, because a board of directors which has any sense of responsibility would want to have its authority coterminus therewith.
By that I mean that to the extent to which you require approval of Governor in Council, you ship the locus of authority beyond the board to the government of the day-and to that extent you erode the character of the company as a private corporation.
I think this is good philosophy and I do not think that Dr. Macintosh would be happy to know that of the 46 clauses in the bill 11 deal with specific powers of the Governor in Council. I asked him about the point concerning the approval or veto of the Governor in Council of the appointment of subsequent presidents. Dr. Macintosh replied, as recorded at page 1951 of the committee proceedings:
As to whether subsequent appointments of president should be so approved, I would have some reservations.
I asked him a good number of questions about the other powers of the Governor in Council, but I think that on this one the point was made quite effectively. I do not think that the government will be prejudiced in its position in the Telesat corporation by allowing a free selection of the president of this body. I think this is an arrogation by the government of powers which they should simply not possess and there is no good reason why they should possess them.
I liken this corporation, if it is to be divided on a one-third, one-third, one-third basis, to two tigers setting up house with a rabbit. One of the tigers is a sabre-toothed tiger and in that respect has an advantage over the other tiger because he has longer teeth. The
June 13, 1963

second tiger is an ordinary tiger and represents the telecommunications industry which probably will be fairly united in its role in this corporation because it is a national system, and the one major group outside the system, in Quebec, is knocking at the door and trying to gain entry into the club. So we have the sabre-toothed tiger-the government -the ordinary tiger-the telecommunications common carriers-and finally the rabbit representing the hundreds or perhaps thousands of Canadian citizens who will be part owners of approximately one-third of Tele-sat. They will be a largely unorganized group, but the rabbit will have to have a fair amount of speed to keep out of the way of the tiger with the long teeth and the tiger with the short teeth. In fact, I suggest that the way this venture is being set up the rabbit will have to have the ability and agility of Bugs Bunny and also his luck to survive this type of operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess that as a result of a combination of too much courtesy this morning and too little agility I lost the place in the order of speakers which is usually reserved for the chief spokesman for the official opposition party. Since there was before the house a government motion asking that this bill be read the third time I thought, in my courtesy, that the minister who is the sky pilot of this legislation might wish to speak first. I also wish to say, having heard the impassioned eloquence of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) in moving his amendment, that I felt the only thing I could do in my righteous indignation was to rush out of the chamber and pull my telephone from the wall and then kick to smithereens my second hand RCA Victor record player in order to show an appropriate attitude toward the vicious princes of privilege to which the hon. member so eloquently referred. Fortunately I was able to restrain myself. I still have telephone service which invariably is far better than the mail service I am getting these days.
In the many sessions of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts we heard interesting and informative witnesses and I appreciate very much the views and special knowledge they placed before us. I also wish to say that in my opinion the chairman of the committee did an excellent job in presiding over that part of the committee's deliberations which dealt with communications. I participated only in those discussions. The witnesses before the committee broadened the knowledge of hon. members. New Vistas were opened and new information was obtained. While much was revealed, Mr. Speaker, much was not revealed and broad areas of uncertainty remain.
While the committee held many meetings and while there was an apparent impatience in some quarters that matters did not proceed with greater dispatch, it should not be forgotten that this is a major undertaking. It is one which will cost Canada many millions of dollars, far more, I fear, than currently estimated. The whole question is one which has important ramifications, both of national and international character. Therefore there is no need for any of us to feel that too much time and effort were devoted to this major, complex and important matter.
It is unfortunate that this most important and most costly project should be launched from a pad of such deep and thick ballyhoo. In the press from time to time have appeared some far-out articles, the writers of which must have been giddy as they allowed their thoughts to orbit with the satellite. Many of the minister's futuristic and glamorous skywriting orations, often given at times of darkest disarray in the Post Office Department, helped to inflate the expectations of some Canadians. References to "blanketing the north" and "giving complete coverage" as well as other inflations of expectations, have certainly clouded the picture and distorted the spectrum.
With the passage of this bill, with the establishment of Telesat Corporation, with the successful launching of the domestic sateUite, very likely from a United States launching pad, there still will not be a colour television set in the domain of every remote dweller in Canada's north. Santa Claus will still not have cradle telephones in his workshops. Putting it very simply, the blanket of the north will still have some very thin spots and quite a few serviceless holes. I therefore feel I must perform a bit of dialectic surgery today, Mr. Speaker.
In the public mind reality is badly mixed with the minister's dreams. The reality ought to be separated from the puffery. Skywriting, I know, is fun. It is so much fun that one usually careful official of the Department of Communications was so uncareful as to say:
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
That is why Canada was one of the first countries to become interested in communications satellites. It promised to solve all our problems.
On a slow press day, talk of newspapers in the home, telescanners, telephones in the sky, all brought by Telesat, will make the front page. It all serves to divert attention from the fact that all last week's papers, brought by

June 13, 1969

the Post Office, will probably arrive at one time, maybe tomorrow.
In the area of costs, we have an example of reality being obscured. The minister tells us in great detail that the Telesat Corporation will be paying out approximately $65 million. This is only part of the story, the whole picture must include other investments. Among those he revealed in the committee sessions which we did not know about before are $43.5 million in investment by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, echo suppressors at $250,000 each, rearward microwave links by carriers at unknown cost. One of the minister's officials estimated that these would cost $500,000 and another gave a more comprehensive figure of $3 million. A fairly significant disparity! I, of course, have no cadre of technical experts to draw upon but must do my best to obtain information from some of the technically and scientifically expert people not in the governmental empire. From estimates I have received I am convinced that it will cost a great deal more than $3 million for the rearward connections to overcome interference for a complete system of satellite telecommunications.
There are definite differences of opinion as to the effect of radar installations on the proper, efficient operation of the satellite system. It is hardly a military secret to indicate that there are some fairly complex pieces of equipment in the Canadian north and also in the north of the United States. There are those with technical competence who believe that it will cost dollars to make the existence of those establishments compatible with the proper operation of the satellite system.
Last April the minister told us, using his now immortal phrase, that we are buying a Volkswagen system instead of a more elaborate Cadillac system. I liked that expression, but I have the painful fear that we just might be getting the Volkswagen on Cadillac terms and Cadillac costs. These estimates, as we try to sort them out, appear to be unsure. Where in the minister's statements of costs of the TV receive-only ground stations does he include the well known principle that construction costs are as much as two and a half times greater in the north than in the south? Why did some of his best officials who have never built a TV broadcast facility underestimate by 40 per cent the figure quoted by the C.B.C. for the essential transmitting facilities? The minister I am sure regards this as an important project. He is determined to bull ahead with it. On one occasion he said that 17 launch failures will not deter him. That is
Telesat Canada Act
interesting. I hope the minister, who is called many things, will not find himself nicknamed the father of the National Arts Centre in the sky.
In another way reality should be distinguished from myth. This project is a heavily subsidized one. Twice taxpayers are asked to subsidize it, through the minister's department and through that of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) who sometimes answers vaguely for the C.B.C. And then taxpayers who have telephones may well be asked to subsidize this system once more through higher rates, and we have had a good deal of discussion about these in the committee.
On April 14 the minister told us that four goals would be met by his Volkswagen system. The first of these goals is to bring television to the north. We have found that there is a good prospect television service will be extended to some of the north and in some other areas in the north television will be improved. In a good many areas of the north many years will pass before they will be watching Don Messer, Bonanza or any of the other old programs, to say nothing of any new ones.
The second goal, improved telephone service to the north, will be met only marginally. It would be very unfortunate if Canadians living in the north ever got the impression that when Telesat is functioning all they will have to do is ring up the nearest telephone company and it will instal a cradle phone right away. The telephone people told us some of the problems they will have. In areas of concentrated population it will come, but this is pretty well the prevailing picture at the present time. We were given figures of the extensive costs for ground stations. Figures were tossed off such as $1.3 million for telephone service alone.
The minister also spoke about the importance of television in two languages for all Canadians. Here perhaps there is an unfortunate mixture of myth and reality. The minister spoke about the new era commencing. We all want an extension of services in both languages across the country, but where are the details? Will Vancouver have a very high frequency French language station? Is Calgary to have such a station? What are the details?
What has to be done to extend the use of French language television outside central Canada? From C.B.C. testimony, it is clear that the same goal could be obtained through existing technology. I think it is passing

June 13, 1969
Telesat Canada Act
strange to hear this minister speak of fostering French language and culture outside of central Canada. Last month he was on a television program. He was there under the gun for ever-increasing postal rates. The minister knows what happened to some French language publications which had circulated outside the province of Quebec. L'E-vangeline of Moncton, in a province that is about 40 per cent French, by the minister's own admission is in serious difficulty because of higher postal rates. It will be in more difficulty when the rates go higher as new stages of imposition are reached.
There was reference to Le Devoir, that great journal of thought and opinion which brings to areas outside of Quebec the thinking of very independent and very able editorial writers. It is strange that this minister holds out such glowing terms of promise of French language television while at the same time he takes away the reality of the expression of French language periodicals.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
His fourth goal-he did not go as far as Presbyterians usually do; he only went to four-establishment of a second and supplementary service to the existing east-west microwave network, is going to be a very important development. On this I only offer the following excerpt from the evidence given to the committee by Mr. Krupski of the Trans-Canada Telephone System, a group who are now on much better terms with the minister than they seemed to be several weeks ago:
The advantages of a satellite system for east-west telecommunications will also be marginal. The existing east-west telecommunications systems are sufficiently ample and diverse to meet all present requirements and are capable of being readily expanded, as needed, to cover the requirements for at least ten years at low incremental cost.
That is another one of the big four. Now I must point out some very important omissions. This bill, full of detail as1 it is in many matters, makes no reference to regulation by statute or by law. I am not so concerned about the extent to which the government is involved in this project. I do not share the fears of some of the members of the N.D.P. The government is there. The minister is there. But parliament is not there. Regulations clearly set out in the statute applicable to this organization and to all bodies in telecommunications1-that is what is missing and that is what should be there. In the white
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
paper it was forecast that it would be there. Page 60 of the white paper reads:
The regulation of a satellite communications system will have to be related intimately with the regulation of terrestrial communications. This is necessary, because of the need to share common radio frequency bands, to avoid wasteful duplication of facilities, and to interconnect all facilities into national and global networks. The regulations must, of course, also provide for communications systems which do not use radio frequencies, for example, cables. There is therefore increasing urgency to develop comprehensive regulatory legislation on telecommunications.
In view of these facts, the government is already inquiring into new legislation which will ensure the comprehensive regulation of telecommunication services, both terrestrial and satellite.
That was the white paper. The date of the white paper was March 28-not 1969 but 1968. Now we are told of a task force, or is it a study group, which is just getting under way. We have had explained to us the establishment of the intradepartmental committee. Apparently only those in the Communications Department are going to be studying this matter, although the question is much broader and covers more than one department. But this group, in comfortable privacy, will be considering the theory which should underpin the regulation of telecommunications.
The minister is very cool and calm about it. It gives him greater ease than smoking, as suggested by the hon. member for York South. He thinks that in three or four years time we should be able to work something out. Mr. Speaker, we are launching a multimillion dollar project and we are told that some time in the future, a few years ahead, we will get around to having regulatory legislation brought forward and passed.
There are many things we have been asking about in recent months. When the Bergeron or Whitehead mission left last fall for a grand tour of Europe we got the impression that it was going to learn many things and tell many things. We have asked many times for its report. Where is it? Was the mission successful?
What is happpening in the negotiations with the C.B.C.? When will we know the price to be charged for the CB.C.'s three channels? Again we ask, what about the discussions with the provinces, especially the province of Quebec which has made certain moves and studies and has made contacts
June 13. 1969

with other countries in reference to this matter? On May 28 the Prime Minister of Quebec told his National Assembly:
As far as Canada is concerned, it appears that they are ready to put some channels at the disposal of Quebec . .. This is all subject to negotiation as to the character, the form, of Quebec's participation. These are all subject to negotiation.
We hope the minister will tell us something about these negotiations. But perhaps more important than anything else I have said before on this whole question is the great lacuna in so far as parliamentary control is concerned. When the minister was asked whether the report of the Telesat Corporation would be subject to parliamentary scrutiny, and be examined by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts his reply in committee on April 22 was:
I would doubt that very much. I stand to be corrected on it, but I think it would be tabled in the house for information. Obviously members could raise questions on it, but could not conduct an examination of it as it is not a Crown corporation.
Later on he said:
Right now I would say, no, but I would like to reserve my answer to that question so I can discuss with my officers all the implications in it. Would that destroy the independent status of the corporation? That is what I would want to assure myself of.
The lack of parliamentary control is a very important matter. There are many questions to be asked.
There is also the question of the location of the stations, how many ground stations there will be, and how much they will cost. When we asked where they would be nobody could tell us. How you can count them and cost them without locating them I do not know.
We look forward to the minister taking us into his confidence in regard to the contracts. He told us on May 20, speaking in the modern jargon which he likes so well:
A critical path, leading to the construction of the satellite itself and its launching, demands that initial contracts for the satellite be given in early May or June.
In effect he said that although the bill is not through one chamber in this parliament, let alone two, and has not received royal assent, these contracts must be initialled in May or June.
Who is receiving the contracts? Has the minister been successful in guaranteeing Canadian content? We would like to know these important things. There is much back-patting about the technological nationalism of
Telesat Canada Act
this project. When we used to say, "What about purchasing an American made bird, which would be cheaper and would probably give better service" we were told, "Canada's independence is worth something." But I wonder about some of the companies to be involved in the building of the Canadian satellite. Will they not be, or some of them, fully owned subsidiaries of U.S. firms? Who will do the launching? And I ask a bit rhetorically, I must confess, are all of the common carriers listed in Schedule A living in a world of virginal detachment from U.S. big business?
So much for the technological and idealogi-cal purity of t'he minister's nationalism in this regard. The bill itself is something less than a fascinating piece of literature. It does not grab one all that dramatically, but it does provide for the government of Canada in one clause to put up $30 million, and in another clause to make a loan up to $40 million, and that is not exactly peanuts even in the Bona-venture era. It is not peanuts in an age when a government can be very sensitive in certain other fields, when a government and a minister can close up a post office with the snap of a finger if it runs behind by a few hundred dollars, when a government can say that even though the P.E.I. causeway would be self-amortizing in a very short time, this is not the time to go into such ventures. In a time of belt-tightening, again I say that sums of $30 million and $40 million are not exactly peanuts.
My hon. friend from Halifax has mentioned the board of directors, perhaps the most pusillanimous board of directors in the history of corporate law. They cannot even elect their own president without government approval. T'he bill is laden with assertions of ministerial or governmental sovereignty and authority, and so I am not worrying about the role of the government or the minister. He will be in there. But there are many other implications in this bill, and especially in the developments which will follow.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Some Canadians perhaps are leery that a man who, to use the kindest expression I can think of, has had an unspectacular career in running the Post Office, should now move into an orbit so much vaster. There is a little quiver of concern, I suppose, when one reflects on the postal zoning fiasco in Canada's major cities, the demise of publications and the disarray of mail service generally. I am prepared to say that the current estimates of

June 13, 1369
Telesat Canada Act
the cost of the satellite system which have been bandied about in the last few weeks and months will soon become as obsolete and useless as the five cent stamp. I have no hesitation in predicting that the $65 million figure will go down in history as the most conservative estimate ever made by a Liberal minister, and there have been some dandies in that category. Why would there not be, because after all the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is a colleague of the Postmaster General and he knows how to do things.
My friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), put a price tag of $200 million on this project before it is through. I do not know how precise his calculations are, but I am inclined to think that 'history will reveal him to be a little better at computing what the future holds for the taxpayers than some of the members sitting on the front benches of his own party.
Having expressed my genuine concern, my anxiety and my continuing desire to have more information on the matter and less bunkum, I can still say I believe I am speaking for the people of Canada and certainly for this party when I say we realize we are now on course, that the measure will become law, and we wish well for those involved in this very important development. We can only hope that all will be well. We hope that the success of the Alouette and ISIS program, rather than the failures of the Post Office, will set the tone for the future of Telesat and other aspects of communications. This is our hope and wish. The scientific communities in this country have done well. We can take pride in their achievements. I believe we all want to encourage technological and industrial innovation and want Canada, if I may use the expression, to maintain a place in the scientific sun. We want all Canadians to get the best service they can in communications, and we in this party even include the written word in communications and would like that to go through as well.
So we of this party do not intend in any way to delay or retard the passage of this measure. We think it might be a good thing if the minister had this bill out of the way so that he might get back to minding the store in the Post Office and perhaps diminish a bit the disarray his previous actions have done so much to encourage. So I say that despite the eloquence of the mover of the amendment I cannot support it. I think there is plenty of the government and plenty of the minister in this measure now. And as I say, as the minister grows wiser and sadder and accepts

some of the changes I have suggested and brings in some improvements in the next few years through decent regulatory legislation, I hope the measure will fly better than we anticipate. We wish him well and want Telesat to succeed now that the decision has been taken.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 15 last, the day after the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) made his speech introducing the motion on second reading of Bill C-184 designed to establish a Crown corporation to be called Telesat Canada, I made a speech in which I dealt especially with the cultural and legal aspects of the setting up of that corporation.
I am still nonplussed, while waiting for the answers to the six specific questions I then put to the minister, about the establishment of the Telesat corporation, more especially in connection with the strategic and extremely important situation of the other Canadian majority, namely that of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for the answer to those questions, not for political purposes, but in order to know the minister's and the government's thinking on Telesat, particularly because of Quebec's position.
We would not want the Telesat corporation to become a source of conflict for Canadians.
I had put the following question: Will the system be bilingual? The minister nods assent, and we would like the bill to provide some guarantee with regard to bilingualism.
I know that the minister answered partially to that question during consideration in committee. At that stage, he gave an eloquent testimony, on which I congratulate him. I was told so, and I read about it, but even if the minister said in the committee that bilingualism will be enforced by Telesat with regard to broadcasting, that is not a written guarantee.
Anyone who is familiar with the history of Canada knows that several things, which were written in the British North America Act, have not been respected.
I wonder how things that are unwritten, that were only mentioned by the minister, will be respected in the future. That is why we would like the minister to consider this request seriously, to amend the bill, to show goodwill, he who was once a Quebec minister, and give such a guarantee to all Frenchspeaking Canadians, because the whole
June 13, 1969

Canadian people are affected by this bill, so that the network reflects truly the image of a Canada which everyone wants, a bilingual Canada, at the very moment when we are in the process of passing the bill on official languages.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I feel this is a significant point, and we can no longer be satisfied with words. We must put in the act specific guaranties with regard to bilingualism, otherwise it will only be another hope or dream, but not a reality. How can we be sure that Tele-sat will truly respect bilingualism? In fact, parliament cannot efficiently control the various Crown corporations, whether they be departmental, agency or proprietary corporations.
The only protection Parliament may secure in regard to Crown corporations is to provide in the act for the protection of bilingualism we want to be recognized by Crown corporations.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the minister's attention to the five other questions, in order that he may give the house the assurance that those questions will actually be answered. To avoid taking up the time of the house, I should like to refer the minister to page 7521 of Hansard for April 15, 1968, where appear the six questions I asked, in the hope that at the end of this debate on third reading, he will enlighten us.
I ask the minister to reconsider those questions, because after reading his evidence before the committee, I feel we do not have any assurance. And much less so, after getting the following answer to question No. 658 I put on the order paper, and I quote:
1. Has an application lor a broadcasting licence by a provincial government or its agents ever been rejected and, if so, when and with respect to what applications and on what grounds?
The answer was as follows:
1. No. The policy of the government, as stated in the House of Commons on May 3, 1946,
Obviously, there is need in this connection for adjustment and updating-
-is still in effect that since broadcasting is the sole responsibility of the federal government, broadcasting licences shall not be issued to other governments or corporations owned by other governments.
This means that the policy in effect since 1946 not only compels the provinces to participate in Telesat and to accept it, but also prevents them from having their own system.

So, if the minister does not answer my questions, it means that he approves of te 1946 policy and thus gives the federal government the right to interfere in the field of education, That is an infringement of the constitutional rights of the provinces which can only intensify the constitutional conflicts at the very time when an attempt is being made to review and revise our constitution.
In addition, the answer stated as follows:
The task force is to study all aspects of this subject in order to assist the government in fulfilling its undertaking to facilitate the development of adequate broadcasting facilities to meet provincial requirements for the transmission of educational programmes. The Task Force will undertake a variety of specific assignments-
-and this is the point I am trying to make-
-and is not asked to produce a comprehensive report.
On the basis of that question which is directly related to the subject under discussion and which also concerns the provinces, the federal government appoints task forces that study the reports of other committees and nothing gets done that way. But as the representatives of the people we cannot obtain a copy of the findings of those so-called experts.
This is why we cannot determine if the minister is sincere when he says that this system will respect bilingualism, the provinces' stand and privileges.
I think that is a basic question. I do not want to turn this into a storm in a tea-cup, but I would merely ask the minister, when he brings the debate to an end-at least we hope so-to enlighten us and dispel the doubts which the Canadian people might still have.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would have some very short comments to make which could be summarized as follows: When we read Bill C-184 now under consideration, we are entitled to ask ourselves certain administrative questions.
In what group under the Financial Administration Act 1952, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 116, would Telesat be classified? This is a legal matter which is not specified in Bill C-184. There is no such provision in the legislation. I think this is a legal mistake and omission that can be fatal.
There are departmental, agency and proprietary Crown corporations. The Corporation's status is not defined in the legislation.
I remember that in his initial speech, the minister merely pointed out that the legal

status of the corporation was very complex. Mr. Speaker, it would certainly be appropriate for the minister and his experts to study this matter more closely and tell us what kind of Crown corporation it is, because it is not defined in the bill. In other words, will the corporation come under the Financial Administration Act? I should like to deal with the audit of financial operations. How will it be conducted? By the Auditor General of Canada?

Would it not be useful if the Auditor General of Canada, who as everybody knows is an official of parliament, the man designated by parliament to audit the financial activities of the Crown Corporations and the departments, a wonderful instrument for hon. members who wish to know the good and bad features of all the administrations, were to audit the books of Telesat? since it must represent all the Canadian people from coast to coast.
Another good thing about this corporation is that the public can share in its financing. Therefore, since the war, the government, through its crown corporations policy, has shown more and more of a trend towards corporations of that type, financed by means of three sources of capital: the government, the public and the private sector.
And the trend-it is irreversible-is more and more towards that, because nationalized enterprises are unable to administer themselves properly and to provide an adequate service. On the other hand, the public does not have access to them. The trend is therefore irreversible, and it allows parliament to exercise a bit more control.
Naturally, everything will depend on the attitude of the minister in this regard, and the replies he will give us. However, we believe in private enterprise and we are happy that Telesat should be the object of legislation in this session, because communications between Canadians from sea to sea must be improved as soon as possible. Those who live in remote regions, the Northwest Territories and other areas, for instance, must have the same cultural, educational and other facilities as Canadians in other areas, and in this connection I wish to congratulate the minister.
In closing I should like to ask him to answer the question I put to him a while ago, not by playing politics but by giving us specific answers and assuring us that the unfortunate situation that exists in the case of Panarctic Oil Ltd, will not recur when Telesat Canada is created.

As I informed hon. members during the committee stage of the bill, discussions have been going on with United States authorities to secure agreement on the necessary launching arrangements. Our objective has been to secure the most efficient and cheapest launching services. For this reason we have never at any time dreamed of encouraging the government to enter into or search for a launching capability of its own; this could easily lead us

into expenditures of some $800 million without any assurance of success.
I am able to say that these discussions with the United States have been satisfactorily completed by an agreement in principle. The necessary technical details will be agreed upon later. I would like to read to hon. members the text of a public statement which has been agreed to by both governments:
Discussions have recently taken place between Canadian and United States authorities concerning launching services required by Canada to place a Canadian communications satellite in synchronous orbit in 1971. The satellite would be used to provide a domestic communications system for Canada, plans for the establishment of which were announced by the Canadian government in the White Paper of April 1, 1968. The U.S. government has indicated that it would be willing to provide the necessary launching services on a cost reimbursable basis pursuant to appropriate arrangements. The Canadian government will be taking appropriate steps in Intelsat to ensure technical compatibility between the Canadian and Intelsat systems and in the ITU in accordance with ITU agreements.
This agreement in principle, which I welcome as evidence of Canada-U.S. co-operation in the vital field of space communications, will enable officials of the two governments to proceed with the necessary, detailed, technical and financial discussions. I would refer to a phrase used by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), "critical path", and say that we are trying to be on target. I do not share the hon. member's pessimism about the cost of this project. Those concerned with the project have worked very closely together, and I am confident that the cost will be less than the $65 million which has been mentioned.
I have today instructed officials of the Department of Communications to open negotiations with RCA Victor Limited of Canada on the procurement contract for Canada's domestic communications satellite. Provided these negotiations result in satisfactory price, quality and performance schedule terms a formal contract will be awarded to RCA Victor. Upon conclusion of these negotiations the contract with RCA Victor would include a direction to award the transponder subcontract to Northern Electric.

These two Canadian firms will thus be responsible for the main elements of the planned domestic communications satellite, the cost of

which is estimated at $25 million to $30 million, exclusive of launcher.
Both RCA Victor and Northern Electric are leaders in the fields of space and telecommunications. It is my information that all of RCA Victor International's expertise in spacecraft telecommunications resides here in Canada. The award of the principal communications satellite contracts will bring significant development both to Canada's communications industry and to our scientific community. Our object is to secure as high a Canadian content as possible, provided the price is right.
RCA Victor would operate as the contractor responsible to Telesat Canada, the tripartite government-private industry-public corporation authority, the creation of which is currently being considered by parliament. The actual construction contracts will be awarded by the corporation.
We have been through an extensive and thorough analysis of the project, both on second reading and particularly in the committee stage.
