speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment presented by the hon. member who has just spoken and a similar amendment presented by myself in exactly the same words-and that by coincidence-to exactly the same purpose-and that is not coincidence-arrived within a few minutes of each other at the Table one day. Perhaps because I am a little farther down the corridor than my hon. friend my amendment arrived in second place, and rather than put Your Honour in the invidious position of having to do a King Solomon in judgment it was decided he would move and I would second his amendment, and the disposition of his amendment would dispose of both amendments. I think that was a reasonable course to take.
Dealing with interest rates I would point out there have been three stages in interest rates relating to national housing. At first they were fixed by statute. In the second stage the formula was varied so that, as my hon. friend has explained, the rate on longterm government borrowings was taken and 2i per cent was added thereto. That was an adjustable interest rate, fixed a certain number of times a year. Finally, there is the proposal in the legislation before us this afternoon to free interest rates from control and allow them find their own level.
The task force on housing headed by the former minister dealt with interest rates on pages 28 and 29 of its report, as noted by my hon. friend. I think this is worth emphasizing again, and I quote directly from the record:
A rise of one percentage point in interest rates adds more than $9 to the monthly payment on a $15,000 "5-year mortgage, raising its total amortization cost by more than $2,800. A two percentage point increase in the same mortgage raises the monthly payment some $19 and the total cost over 25 years by about $5,700. These are hardly insignificant amounts. Nor do they tell the whole story. Developers and builders operate on credit, too. When their cost of money, short or longterm, is high, they have no alternative but to reflect this increasing cost in higher prices for their product.
So there is a multiplying effect in what higher interest rates can do. The task force goes on to say there are no simple solutions in dealing with interest rates, and one has to concede that. But then the task force, with this in mind, says categorically at the bottom of page 28 of its report:
Mortgage interest rates must come down.
June 13. 1969	COMMONS
Then there is the recommendation which has found its way into this legislation, and I quote:
To ensure a more continuous and even flow of mortgage funds and in the hope the N.H.A. rate might well decline, the task force therefore recommends that:
The interest rate for insured loans under the National Housing Act be freed to find its own level in the financial market place.
I suggest that the key words there are "in the hope" and "might well decline." There is certainly a hope that they might decline but I think it is a very fanciful hope.
A few years ago we dealt with the Bank Act and the formula for interest rates contained therein. The proposal brought before us removed the 6 per cent interest rate ceiling on loans made by chartered banks. This was to allow them to compete with the nonbank finance intermediaries and also to allow those rates to find their own level in the marketplace. The late hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked during that debate, as recorded at page 8419 of Hansard for October 6, 1966:
Do I take It from that, that the minister anticipates that if restraints were taken off immediately, there would immediately be a dislocating jump in interest rates?
The then minister of finance, who is now cultivating the junior Chinese diplomatic community in Europe, replied:
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I said that I felt there would be apprehension on this score.
That was the strongest quotation we could find in recent years in our research dealing with the removal of the ceiling on interest rates. I repeat again what the Minister of Finance said:
Mr. Speaker, I said that I felt there would be apprehension on this score.
Since the ceiling was removed we know what has happened to bank interest rates. We have received some pretty rude reminders in the last few days of what can happen to interest rates.
The hon. member for Broadview was good enough to compliment my leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition, who would have liked to take part in the vote that it is expected will take place on this amendment. Unfortunately he has to attend a political convention of some considerable dramatic import in the province of New Brunswick. I should like to quote what the Leader of the Opposition
National Housing Act, 1954 said in the house on June 2 this year as reported in Hansard at page 9339 with regard to the very problem with which we are dealing this afternoon. He said:
What government having at heart the best interests of the Canadian householder would seriously consider at this time removing the interest ceiling on C.M.H.C. mortgages and abolishing the maximum differential permitted between long term government of Canada interest rates and the maximum that may be received with respect to mortgages?
I am referring to government guaranteed loans in connection with housing. What government thinking of the ordinary Canadian would consider doing this when we see increasing indications that money is to be in short supply and that there is to be competition for available dollars? There is every indication that interest rates will rise further.
That prophecy has certainly been realized and in a remarkable short period of time.
Indeed, rates have been rising so steadily that one can take increased rates almost for granted. Our expectations in this regard are fortified by predictions.
I know that orthodox finance is in favour of taking off the ceiling. I say that orthodox finance is not always right. If the government takes the position it is necessary to remove the ceiling in order to get more money into housing, that at least is an honest position, although it would probably result in people paying higher interest rates. But for the government of Canada to put forward this proposal and seriously suggest at this time, in view of the current and anticipated conditions in the money markets, that removing the interest ceiling will lower interest rates on C.M.H.C. loans is pure folly. If the government cannot do something to help poor Canadians, for goodness sake do not make things worse.
Those were the words of the Leader of the Opposition. I think everyone who is concerned about the effect of what we are being asked to do by this legislation will take those words very seriously indeed.
I should like to make two points with regard to interest rates. First, they have not generally been up to the maximum ceiling permitted in the formula that has been in effect for the last two years or so. They have been a bit below, so there has been some dampening effect, I suggest, in having such a formula in use.
The second point I wish to make is that these loans are insured so that a large element of the risk is thereby automatically dissipated for the mortgage lender. He cannot possibly lose by investing his money in mortgages under the housing scheme covered by National Housing Act mortgages. So I suggest there is a great deal of difference between taking money and investing it in the housing field and investing it even in the common stocks of Canadian commercial companies. I
June 13, 1969

National Housing Act, 1954 think there is a big difference indeed. It is the principle of insured loans and the almost negligible risk which I think is important and one the government is losing sight of in bringing in this measure at this time.
Finally, sir, there is the cost factor involved. I suggest that 40-year mortgages with interest rates the way they are now place people in an almost impossible financial quandary. This places a terrible financial burden on the backs of the people which they will carry from the time they enter the housing market, say at the age of 20 or 25 years, until they retire at the age of 60 or 65 years. That is a full working lifetime in which they will have to carry the tremendous burden of high interest and mortgage costs. I suggest there must be people who are clever enough to devise a formula. There are certainly people around who have heart and who would want a formula to be devised and who would agree that housing is one of the necessities of life.
I believe we should have a housing program and a philosophy that will ensure that our young people can become a part of it when they start out initially. I say "initially" because the term appeals to me. If a person wishes to wander from house to house like a nomad taking part in speculative enterprises that is one thing, but the person who wants to have decent shelter should not be saddled with ferocious costs involving a second mortgage with rates anywhere from 16 per cent to 24 per cent. I suggest that it is a social necessity to give young people a break in this country. I do not think I am exaggerating the situation in any way. We are exaggerating it by the formula the minister suggests to us in this bill.
The fact is that 80 per cent of the people of Canada want to own their own single family homes. It is also a fact that the number of single family starts in relation to all housing construction has declined steadily. One could almost say that 80 per cent of the people could not under any circumstances now own a single family dwelling. That is the pity; that is the tragedy. That is the reason this amendment comes before the house this afternoon and is going to be supported.

It is no secret that many wildlife conserva-tionalists, and those people concerned with pollution in the province of British Columbia, have expressed strenuous reservations about the devastation to the landscape and the ecological upset that strip mining operations of this kind will cause.
This particular bill provides for transportation service for just that portion-a vast area in this region-which has been marked for exploitation by those interested in the strip mining of coal. I think it is important to record here just how extensive this area is. An area of some 80 square miles is already under lease from the province of British Columbia, that is licences have already been granted to three separate coal companies. This amounts to 50,000 acres so far, and there probably is more to come once we pass this rail line extension legislation. Fifty thousand acres of mountains and the best wildlife habitat in British Columbia will be destroyed forever in the name of industrial progress and the gross national product. A fifty thousand acre area for hunting, recreation and tourism now risk erosion and the exposure of the substrata, which will carry pollution and harmful substances into the nearest creek.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
What will be done with the product mined in this region? I think this is an important question which we 'have to examine. It will, of course, be shipped through the Roberts Bank super port in its raw state, to serve the industrial demands of the secondary industries of Japan. British Columbia will continue its historical pattern of dependence upon an extraction industry and primary industrial base, like some northern banana republic, exporting our resources and extending

June 13, 1969
Private Bills
secondary industrial employment opportunities to some other country. What will the province of British Columbia receive for all this ravage? As I understand it, the royalties amount to 50 cents per acre, whereas Kentucky, which has had 50 years experience with these kinds of coal company depredations, charges $25 per acre. Because of its history and unhappy experience with King Coal, Kentucky has developed much more stringent state mining legislation than that which the province of British Columbia has enacted.
I am well aware that any person or group attempting to place a higher value on wildlife and landscape conservation than on an industrial operation of this magnitude will be considered either a sentimentalist or a kook. I am aware, too, that if you live in that region and need a job, you need it right now and not in the future. This area has been in desperate economic straits for years. Many of the people living there welcome these new developments because they will provide an economic transfusion and improve local employment prospects.
I think the attitude in the area is something like this: The people say, "We've been poor long enough. Lord, we don't need another mountain, and to hell with a few elk; let's move them somewhere else". I can appreciate how they feel. But in any of these major developments does anybody ever think of instituting ecological cost-benefit studies so that the public can be assured that it is to everyone's long term advantage to proceed; or do we always, on the contrary, rush to obtain the fast buck and leave the future to take care of itself?
I would like for a moment to ask a few questions about clause 3 of the bill which deals with the Fraser Valley or Roberts Bank end of the line. Hon. members will recall that last fall when we attempted to gain information from the then Minister of Transport regarding the rail routes through the Fraser Valley to serve the new super port, we were informed that since this new line was internal to British Columbia and the national railways not involved, there was no federal interest in the matter.
I think the lower mainland members particularly will also recall that the municipalities through which the line was to pass were picked off one by one and kept in the dark about the precise route until it was too late to do anything about it. It must also be said that because of the aggressive stand taken by the 
Lower Mainland Regional Planning Board to the Roberts Bank route, the planning board itself-probably the best in Canada-became the first victim of this new rail line. It was chopped into four pieces so that it would become less troublesome to the provincial government, even though the board was itself a creature of that government. When it became time to evaluate a particular rail line as opposed to planning in the lower Fraser Valley, the rail line won and the planning board was out. Clause 3 of the bill provides as follows:
The company-
That is Canadian Pacific Railway.
-upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon by the directors of the respective companies, may enter into an agreement to purchase an interest in and may operate its trains over such lines of railway as the British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority may construct in the province of British Columbia.
After being assured last fall that there was no national railway interest in this line, suddenly, through the back door so to speak of Bill S-31, we find that at least one national railway has a very real interest in the line, because the bill uses the words "purchase an interest in". There may be nothing very sinister in this, Mr. Speaker, but Canadians have a right to be cynical about the activities of Canadian Pacific Railway. I think it is fair to say that all railways operating in the lower mainland of British Columbia have an understandable desire to be assured access to the super port. There are two rail lines other than the C.P.R. and the hydro railway operating in this region.
Clause 3 may mean that the C.P.R. is going to finance the new Hydro extensions in return for lower running rights charges. This may be sensible financing on the part of the provincial government. On the other hand, we do not know at this point how much interest in the line they intend to purchase. In spite of all our efforts in the committee, we were unable to obtain this information. If it were 10 per cent or 25 per cent, no one would be particularly concerned; but if it is 51 per cent, which would represent a controlling interest, I think everyone has a right to be concerned because it then becomes a federal matter. What are the terms of this so-called agreement which is to be negotiated? In our committee hearings we were unable to ascertain anything at all in this respect. This is our major concern; we wonder what equity the C.P.R. will have, and whether they will have a controlling interest. I believe all hon.
June 13, 1369

members have a right to know the answers to these questions, because Bill S-31 is the enabling legislation in this regard and through its provisions Canadian Pacific will be able to at least purchase an interest in the hydro railway.
Having said all these things, Mr. Speaker, it would be a very simple matter for members of this party, or any other for that matter, to talk this bill out today or on subsequent days. We could do all kinds of unpleasant things to the bill in order to delay its passage. We could cause all kinds of trouble to the companies involved, including the possible loss of coal contracts. However, we shall not do this.
The responsibility for the leases, the strip mining, the erosion, the loss of wildlife, tourists, and the rail lines rests squarely on the shoulders of the provincial government. It must be emphasized that resources, as members of the house know, are strictly a provincial matter. They are fully the responsibility of the province, and theirs alone. We are not going to be manoeuvred into a position of employing what is really just a delaying tactic-it could be described as a rearguard action-with regard to this enabling legislation which will provide access to leases already signed by the provincial government.
I think that it is enough that we point out the possible inherent dangers and ultimate costs. It is enough that we tell the people of British Columbia, through this house, who is directing the show. If the citizens of British Columbia find that this is not what they want in terms of their environmental future, I believe they will know exactly who to blame and how to express their dissatisfaction at the appropriate time at the appropriate ballot box.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly on this bill. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) has covered most of the points with which I would have dealt. First of all, I should like to draw attention to clause 3 of the bill. It is a matter of concern to me that we were not allowed to raise this issue in the house because it was not a federal matter pertaining to the railway system. Now, we find that once the B.C. hydro has built part of this rail line to Roberts Bank, the C.P.R. will be able to purchase part of it. Certainly, this information must have been available several months ago when this issue was before the house. I feel that members of this house
Private Bills
should have had an opportunity to discuss this issue at that time. However, I am not going to say much more about it. I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley West has covered this point rather adequately.
I should like to deal with one or two other clauses of the bill, one of them dealing with the 34 mile railway spur which is to be built up the Elk River and the Fording River. I think we are in a rather awkward position. I believe that a great amount of questioning research would have had to be done on it had it come before the provincial legislature. Here, in Ottawa, we find that provincial governments let mineral and timber leases, and then when access is required by a rail line or perhaps some company wishes to build a road on land that is leased-in this case it is a rail line-the matter comes under our jurisdiction. I think that the provincial governments owe it to the people under their jurisdiction to make certain that when leases are granted, they are granted in the best interests of the people of the province. Nobody can convince me that a royalty of 50 cents per acre of coal land is a good return to the general public. Mind you, there are other indirect returns from the economic development of these resources which we do not take into consideration at this time. The hon. member quoted the difference between the royalties paid in this area and some that had been paid in the United States, and there is absolutely no comparison.
These old leases were let many years ago by the provincial authorities, and they have nothing to do with this house. Unfortunately, we are not in a position to go to the provincial government and demand that a better return be made to the general public because these mistakes were made many years ago.
Again, we are in a very awkward position here. There is no doubt in my mind that this strip mining venture will pollute both the Elk and the Fording rivers. However, the pollution of these rivers is a provincial responsibility and can and should be stopped by the provincial authorities. This is the awkward position in which we find ourselves when we consider this bill.
There is one more thing I should like to say. It seems to me that when we have a number of very fine areas with good coal resources it does not make too much sense to jump all over the country making a start on half a dozen mines. If there were proper development of the present coal resources, we could cut down pollution to the minimum.

June 13, 1969
Private Bills
Again, I will point out to the sponsors of the bill that this is a provincial responsibility.
There is one point that I would like to make before concluding my remarks. It seems to me that it can apply both federally and provincially. It is really a challenge to wise resource management and it should be applied in this area. Possibly some assistance should be given by the federal authorities with regard1 to wise resource management in the Elk and Fording river area because the waters from these rivers flow into the Kootenay River and eventually end up in the Columbia which, of course, is an international river and as such comes under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities.
I agree with my colleague that a committee or a major task force should be set up to evaluate the feasibility of reclamation in south eastern British Columbia and to consider the effects of surface mining techniques, including erosion, acid water production, sediment production, slides, highwalls, and the feasibility of revegetation. I think there should be a joint study, federal and provincial, in this regard. It could be a good guideline for projects which no doubt will be started in other parts of Canada at a later date.
I think that a special study should also be initiated-again by both the federal and provincial authorities-to consider the effects of surface mining on fish, wildlife, plants and aquatic insects, and that funds and staff be provided for this project immediately. I also believe that this study should include the effects on the Libby reservoir of sedimentation and pollution from the mining operations in the Elk Valley. There is no reason why the federal and provincial governments should not have a joint study of the two aspects which I outlined briefly.
There is just one more thing I would like to say before sitting down. We realize, especially in this area, the need for economic development. Jobs will be provided by the opening up of areas such as this. But again I want to point out that the responsibility for proper protective measures must come mainly from the provincial authorities. The responsibility for a proper return to the provincial purse must fall upon the provincial authorities.
I should like to conclude by saying that we will let this bill pass, and I trust that organizations in British Columbia will use all the persuasive powers they have to make certain that the companies involved, and the provincial government especially, live up to the

strip mining regulations recently laid down by the province of British Columbia. I trust that the people in the area will be satisfied with the results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since we are resuming consideration of Bill C-192 on the National Housing Act, and more specifically of the rather similar amendments which have been moved, I will say now that we will certainly support them because it is a matter of helping those in need of housing.
Mr. Speaker, we will never do enough in the area of housing for that is one of the most important factors for the development and growth of the human being and of the family.
June 13, 1969	COMMONS
Human beings have to be protected and, therefore, must live in decent housing.
In our society we have everything necessary to build houses, to give our families suitable dwellings.
This bill is a severe setback since the already sky-high ceiling on interest rates has been lifted.
It seems to me that big finance is left free to do as it pleases. It was believed in the past that the removal of ceilings would bring about competition between financiers and that interest rates would fall in the process.
We saw what happened when we amended the Bank of Canada Act and the Chartered Banks Act. We were asked to get rid of the ceiling on interest rates, and almost all Liberal, Progressive Conservative and New Democratic members of parliament agreed at that time, saying that upping the interest ceiling was a logical course of action since rates would decrease as a result of greater competition.
But what happened was quite the opposite. We fought with all our might. We raised every possible objection, but the interest rates continued to climb. In fact, all financiers have increased the interest rates, thus reducing the purchasing power of citizens, raising the cost of living, causing inflation and further annoying all Canadian citizens.
As far as housing is concerned, it is illogical to abolish the ceiling on interest rates, because I think it should not go over 3 per cent. Here, in this house, we should adopt a rule, since it is one of the most important factors, in order to give the individual what he needs and what he is entitled to, his dwelling, his property, a home port, if you want. The Canadian citizens must be in a position to return to their home port as often as they wish. This is where the family recuperates. It is there also that the head of the family or those in charge of the family recover their courage and their drive to be able to work, to build, to raise a family properly and to do their personal and civic duties.
If we do not have that, we will prevent the development of the Canadian family and of the individuals.
Mr. Speaker, what is being done now in the field of housing, I ask you? Legislation is brought in to develop that sector, it is claimed, when it is only to help the damned finance, if you will pardon the expression, Mr. Speaker. Big finance is being helped, not the people when such legislation is introduced. People, human beings and the family
National Housing Act, 1954 are exploited. The Liberals accept this exploitation of the family through such stupid legislation and through offensive, cruel, stupid and even criminal regulations.
Here is what I read recently in a newspaper, and I quote:
You buy a $24,000 house? Then, you can boast of having purchased a $84,000 house rather than a $24,000 one. Yes, because with a $20,000 mortgage over 30 years at 9| per cent, you will have paid as much as $60,000 in interest in thirty years. And so your house will cost you $34,000.
If someone buys that house and gives $4,000 cash, then a $24,000 house costs $60,000 in interest, at 9| per cent. When the rate of interest is 11 and 12 per cent, and the loan is to be repaid over 40 years, interest charges go up to $110,000 or $120,000 for a $24,000 house.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Does that make any sense to you, Liberal members? Are those laws and regulations really meant to help and protect human beings or that damned finance? That is what you are working for. That is what you are doing. Those are the great regulations you offer the people but they will not forget.
People have the right to live and Canadian citizens have the right to adequate housing, since construction materials exist, engineers are available and the unemployed are ready and willing to build houses. It is because we do not have the necessary money, because credit is limited, and because we refuse to lend one red cent if it does not yield 10, 12, 15, 24 per cent in interest; thus, big finance is protected at the expense of the taxpayers, of those in need of a roof over their head.
In a logical economy a Canadian citizen who wants to build a house should be able to pay it in ten years. Such a house should not cost more than $10,000 for an ordinary worker; yet it costs $18,000 to $25,000 at the present time. There is swindling everywhere, not only with regard to the cost of building materials but also with regard to taxes levied by the government on those building materials. A lot is said about those taxes, but they are not abolished.
Canadians are encouraged to build houses by being told: Instead of lending you $15,000 or $18,000, we will lend you $25,000 and we will extend the repayment term to 40 years. We have never seen such a catastrophic situation as far as housing is concerned, and the government has the nerve to tell the Canadian people that they help the humble folk, that
June 13, 1969

National Housing Act, 1954 they improve the legislation to help the poor to improve their lot, to help them to build decent houses, when nobody will be able to build one, except those to whom finance will advance money, because they earn $15,000, $18,000 or $20,000 a year. In a little while, even those who earn such a salary will be unable to get a suitable house for themselves.
Therefore, some improvements should be made. The Liberals will not do it, because they are too devoted to partisanship and not one of them will denounce the dreadful things attributable to big finance. There are several Progressive Conservatives who would also be reluctant to do so.
We have been elected by the people to administer its property and to give it protection. Only 10 per cent of the population are represented by the big financiers who control credit. Then, instead of taking the side of the population which represents 90 per cent of those who elected you, you prefer to go along with the 10 per cent that is exploiting the people. That is what the Liberals are doing. That is the direction they have taken so far, and it is under such conditions that the Liberals have governed the country up to the present time.
There will certainly be an end to this, perhaps a tragic end, but I shall not be responsible because I have done my duty. If you did the same, we could perhaps avoid such difficulties or avoid the dreadful things that are coming.
Canadians are living in a free country, yet, building materials are not being put to use and nothing is done about the unemployed. No effort is being made to adopt proper regulations and laws and to find the required techniques to build houses at a low cost. Nothing at all is done about all those things. The only thing that is being done is getting organized so that costs may be as high as possible, so that financial institutions may make as much money as possible. To hell with families! To hell with children! To hell with society! That is the goal you are after, you of the Liberal party, with this housing legislation.
Things cannot go on like that forever and the end may come sooner than you think.
I ask you to take your responsibilities as I take my own, and to condemn such a terrible situation.
I do not like to say such things. I do not like to hurt other citizens who are as honest as I am, and who would like also to live in a more perfect and more humane society. It

hurts me to tell them that. Many among you entertain a spritit as humanitarian as mine but you do not have the intestinal fortitude to do what I am doing.
Every elected member should work in that frame of mind and we should organize the economic realities to make them more practicable, more human, so as to provide for all possible opportunities in a country such as Canada, with its tremendous wealth, where the increasing population is entitled to the benefits of technology, science and progress.
The people are entitled to all those things and that is why we should work and combine our efforts to that end so that a just society may prevail. If we worked to that effect we could say that we are doing something and we could commend you instead of blaming you. We are blaming you because what you are doing does not make sense.
Mr. Speaker, I would have a lot more to add but, in closing, I thank you and once more I ask those who still have some conscience left to get hold of themselves and to do everything which is humanly possible in order to improve the situation and to provide for the appropriate and normal development of our Canadian family through technical and scientific progress and everything else we can make available to it.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT, 1954 AMENDMENTS CLARIFYING DEFINITIONS AND DEALING WITH THE INTEREST RATE ON INSURED LOANS, AND OTHER MATTERS- REPORT STAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief. I do not think I can be as fiery as the previous speaker was. I have always taken the position that when we are elected to this house we represent first Canada, then our province, then our constituency. I hope I may be excused for talking about Calgary this afternoon but there are certain matters I should like to bring to the attention of the house.
At the present time we are considering an amendment to Bill C-192, clause 2 of which has to do with the removing of the ceiling on interest rates. The amendment seeks to delete that clause and to protect the people of Canada who wish to purchase homes. In this country it has been difficult for people to obtain money for down payments and mortgages. It might be well to consider for a moment what has been done in the United States. In that country, when citizens need money for any purpose they set up a special type of corporation and various citizens subscribe varying amounts of money towards that corporation. A ceiling of $10,000 or $20,000 is often set
June 13, 1969	COMMONS
with respect to amounts being invested. Citizens of Canada could set up similar corporations. I submit that interest earned from money invested in such corporations should not be subject to income tax. The money put into such corporations would earn a reasonable rate of interest and the people who are shareholders of the corporations could, within a reasonable time, accumulate quite a large chunk of money which could be used for house building or any other good purpose. It would be a case of average people helping average people. That is one way to solve our housing crisis. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) was good enough to listen to my suggestion with respect to grain. I hope the government will also consider the suggestions I have been making in my remarks, since our people need all the help they can get in solving the housing crisis.
I wish to deal with a second matter that affects Calgary. Since the second world war the city of Calgary has been developing at a rapid pace. It has a population of almost 400,000 people now, if one includes the suburbs. At the outbreak of war, the population of the city was between 60,000 and 70,000 people. Its growth has been brought about as a result of affluence over a long period of time in our agricultural, ranching and petroleum industries. Also, secondary industries which have sprung up in this city have helped to increase its pace of development. Many of those secondary industries depend on the primary industries which originally brought about the expansion of the area. It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that four hon. members of this house represent ridings that are closely related to the city of Calgary. We have the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Harkness), who is our senior member; I represent the constituency of Calgary North; a Liberal hon. member represents the riding of Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) and, of course, we have the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher). We four represent the city of Calgary here.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We must ask ourselves one question at this time, Mr. Speaker. Why should the city of Calgary be brought before the bar of this house and tried for being too successful. This course reminds me of a criminal being brought before the bar of justice and told, you are guilty. The city of Calgary is guilty because it has been successful. It has developed into a fine industrious city. The people

National Housing Act, 1954 are basically average people and fairly affluent. The city has its pockets of poverty, like any other urban city, and has its rich. Some credit must be given to governments at all levels for stimulating the industries to which I am referring.
This government talks about changing the constitution. I never knew the constitution of Canada or any new constitution would be such that it would make an exception of any selected area which had been able to become successful through its initiative and ability to create. This is what is being done with Calgary, Toronto and other urban centres. The government stated it was making a certain kind of budget to apply to those areas which will affect housing, interest rates and, in fact, the whole economy. The government states this budgetary provision will apply to one area of Canada and not another.
By amending the constitution and using the budget, the government has stated the city of Calgary will now come under a different financial law than some of its neighbours. Let us take a look at how ridiculous this system is. I will use a practical example such as a bank building. The decision to build a bank building in the city of Calgary does not result from the deferment of depreciation for two years on a building to be built in Pictou county where they do not require that kind of building. Under this system of selectivity, the government has changed the constitution and the whole economic tone of the city. I would have thought that would have been sufficient. That was the first crack we received last week from this government of the just society.
I would have thought the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) would have been pretty upset with that one piece of bad news. What has the government done now? The minister responsible for housing is in the house and he can deny the information I have. I wish the hon. member for Calgary South were here at this moment. He is away on official business and is absent for no other reason. By not being here, he is probably doing a better job than I am doing at this moment. Maybe it is better that he is not here because it is difficult for a government backbencher to get up in this house and attack the government. That can only be done in caucus. The only trouble with that procedure is it is like winking at pretty girls you never see. Unless what you are doing gets back to your constituents, they do not know that you are working. However, that is politics.
June 13, 1969

National Housing Act, 1954 Let's take a look at what the government has done to housing in Calgary. I received a very long wire from the city council. They are worried about both these matters. I have also received a wire from the chamber of commerce. The minister said part of the news release that went out was true and part was untrue. I know what the minister is doing. He is delaying the cancellation of the need for urban development in the city of Calgary until we go home June 27. When the house is closed, he will then make the announcement, just as the government did with respect to NATO. He thinks that once he plays a trick on the opposition, he can try a new one tomorrow.
Everyone is wondering how much more western Canada can take from the government. It almost appears as though this government is trying to see that never again is a Liberal elected in western Canada. I agree with that. It is the only part of the government's policy that is worth while. I quote from the news release:
Usually reliable sources here say that the federal minister responsible for housing, Robert Andras, has decided to turn thumbs down on all urban renewal projects across Canada except four-at the most five.
I received a copy of this Scott report from Calgary.
From what I can gather, there's one in the west, at Ladner near Vancouver; two in Ontario, one of them Sault Ste. Marie, and one on the east coast, St. John's, Newfoundland-a fifth may get last minute approval.
This is what the report says. These are not my words.
But it is certain that Pat Mahoney, the only government M.P. from Calgary, was given the bad news a few days ago.
This does not mean he is the only member but he is the only one who was given the bad news a few days ago.
The mayor of Drumheller was here seeing the housing minister, Mr. Andras, on Monday, and he apparently learned that the urban renewal project for Newcastle and Naemine will remain in the freeze along with the whole of east Calgary. Sources say the government feels large and largely commercial renewal projects are just too expensive for municipalities at today's interest rates; Ottawa wants to put its money into low rental housing and condominium housing projects, not commercial redevelopment. The urban renewal limbo will be in effect for at least two years. The government is springing the long awaited announcement on Canada's municipalities at the end of the first week in July after M.P.'s have returned home or headed out on vacation. The urban renewal cancellation comes as a second blow to western cities in the midst of a building boom: the first being the

Benson budget which defers depreciation for two years on all commercial development in Calgary and Edmonton.
I don't know how much more socialistic than that you can get, and I say that in a philosophical sense. The government is trying to say this provision will equalize things. What this system means is that since there are pockets of poverty throughout this country and a lack of development for one reason or another, the government is going to start implementing laws through the budget affecting housing production in order to give people the opportunity to live in dignity. It intends to reduce to a poverty level cities such as Calgary and Toronto, some of the best areas in Canada. This is what the Liberal party is doing. They do not want success in the whole nation. They feel Calgary is too successful.
The pay-off came when I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) a question. This is the best answer that has ever been given since Mackenzie King said there would not be one five cent piece for unemployment. Either the minister did not understand my question or he was being brutally frank about reducing certain areas to poverty. I want to make sure this is on the record. The question I asked on June 4 appears at page 9729 of Hansard. It reads:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. The question is serious and arises out of the budget. Is the government giving any consideration to the economic fact that the budgetary measures in regard to the deferral of capital cost allowances will slow development in Toronto, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver, and in particular increase unemployment in those areas, as well as rents that are already high?
I said this would cause unemployment in Calgary because the skilled and unskilled men, 30 per cent of our labour force, are now engaged in the building of comercial buildings. These have now been hit by the Benson budget through deferred depreciation. Who will put their money into these projects if depreciation is not allowed?

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the amendment before us, I wish to say at the outset that I have considerable sympathy with the feelings and the depth of concern expressed and inherent in the amendment itself. Having said this, I have to add that from all I have heard nothing would suggest that the restoration of the ceiling on interest rates could do other than inhibit the flow of funds into the residential mortgage market, which is the thing we want to avoid at this time.
There has been a suggestion that we should restore the interest ceiling on mortgage funds to a level of 2J per cent above the long-term government bond yield, adjusted every quarter. 10132	COMMONS DEBATES	June 13, 1969

To the hon. members who propose the action inherent in the amendment I suggest that in order to make it stick, or make it valid, they would have to go into a much more comprehensive form of control of the economy than this type of "ad hocery" would suggest. In other words, funds going into the residential mortgage market will be meeting investment competition from other sectors, and to make the residential mortgage market competitive with other forms of investment they would have to go so far as to consider controls on the yields of such other investments. This would inevitably lead to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has indicated would be a closed economy, and we would inevitably have to face up to the possibility of controlling and pegging wages, prices and profits. That would be a totally restricted economy, and I do not think anyone is ready to take that kind of action at this time.
I also believe that in order to assure the flow of mortgage funds into the residential market under a controlled ceiling we would have to go even further than what I have suggested. We would have to look into arbitrary legislation to control and regulate the amount of funds that the various lenders would have to put in, to make sure these were adequate, under a fixed rate of interest.
But even if these things worked in Canada, in spite of the fact that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) says that international monetary matters and interest rates really do not affect the mortgage market in this country, I really do not think we could stand in isolation from the kind of events that are distressingly taking place elsewhere in the world. We are all aware of the increased interest rates in the United States. We are all aware of the turmoil in which European money markets find themselves. Just the other day the daily rate for Euro dollars went as high as 12 J per cent. All this has a bearing on our own situation in Canada. We just cannot exist in isolation from other countries.
